title: Airbnb
brief: Design a home-rental marketplace like Airbnb: hosts list places, guests search by area and dates and book a stay. Search must understand both where and when, and a listing must never be booked twice for the same night. Guests pay up front and hosts get paid after check-in.

functional: Hosts create a listing and manage its calendar and prices.
Guests search by place, dates, guests and filters.
A guest books a listing for a range of nights and pays.
Hosts get paid after the stay starts.
Guests and hosts review each other after the stay.
Guests and hosts message each other.

nonFunctional.name: Search latency
nonFunctional.target: Results in under 300 ms at the 99th percentile

nonFunctional.name: No double booking
nonFunctional.target: A listing night is booked by at most one guest

nonFunctional.name: Booking safety
nonFunctional.target: A retry never charges or books twice

nonFunctional.name: Availability
nonFunctional.target: Search stays up at 99.95%, even if slightly stale

nonFunctional.name: Money
nonFunctional.target: Every charge and payout is traceable and reconciled

estimate.note: Assumptions, not facts. Searches vastly outnumber bookings, and the calendar is one row per listing per night, which is a big table even though each row is tiny.

outputs.label: Searches per second at peak
outputs.note: Each one is a geo, date and filter query.

outputs.label: Bookings per second at peak
outputs.note: Few, but each is a correctness-critical write.

api.does: Returns a page of listings in the area that are free for those nights, with total price.
Returns listing details, a live availability check and a price quote.

api.call: POST /bookings  { listingId, checkin, checkout, quoteId } + Idempotency-Key
api.does: Holds the nights, charges the guest, confirms. A repeat key returns the same booking.
Host blocks nights or changes nightly prices.
Allowed once, only after a completed stay.

data.fields: listingId, hostId, lat, lng, type, amenities, capacity, rules
data.why: The source of truth for details, edited by hosts. Search copies the fields it needs into its index.

data.store: Store with conditional writes, key listingId + date.
data.why: One row per night. Booking is a conditional write: set booked only where status is free. That is the double-booking guard.

data.fields: bookingId, listingId, guestId, range, total, status, idemKey
data.why: Money and state changes need transactions. A unique idemKey makes booking safe to retry.
Written once per stay, read per listing. Hidden until both sides submit or a deadline passes.

evolution.title: One app, one database
evolution.problem: Start with what works: one server and one relational database for listings and bookings.
evolution.change: Search is a SQL query on city and filters. Booking inserts a row if no booking overlaps.

evolution.title: A geo search index
evolution.problem: Searching by map area plus amenities, price and type means range scans on latitude and longitude plus many filters. SQL cannot answer that fast with millions of listings.
evolution.change: Build a search index of listings with a geo structure and filter fields, fed from the database by a change stream. Search returns listing ids ranked, and details come from the database. Nearby search is a known block, shown here as one node.

evolution.title: A calendar with availability
evolution.problem: A search for 3 nights must not show listings that are already booked. Date overlap does not fit a text or geo index well, and a listing is free or busy per night.
evolution.change: Keep a calendar store with one row per listing per night. Search finds nearby candidates, then checks them against the calendar in a batch and drops the booked ones. Part of this can be copied into the index to prune early.
evolution.numbers: the estimator shows rows and GB

evolution.title: A booking service with conditional writes
evolution.problem: Two guests pick the same Friday and both pass the availability check. A plain check then write lets both succeed, and one guest arrives to a stranger in the flat.
evolution.change: A booking service writes the nights in one conditional transaction: set each night to held only where it is free. Exactly one writer wins, and the other gets 'dates no longer available'. A hold expires if payment is not completed.

evolution.title: Payments and host payouts
evolution.problem: Booking takes money. A retry must not charge twice, and the host should not be paid before the guest arrives or if the stay is cancelled.
evolution.change: Charge the guest with an idempotency key, then confirm the booking and publish Confirmed on a queue. A payout worker pays the host after check-in, with a ledger entry per step. Refunds follow the cancellation policy.

evolution.title: Pricing as its own service
evolution.problem: The price depends on the night (weekends, seasons), the length of stay, guest count and fees. Search needs a total for every result, and the guest must pay exactly what they saw.
evolution.change: A pricing service reads nightly prices from the calendar, applies discounts and fees, and returns a quote with an id. Booking charges the quote, so the price cannot shift between page and payment.

evolution.title: Reviews and messaging
evolution.problem: Trust drives bookings. Reviews must come only from real stays, and guests and hosts must talk before and after a booking.
evolution.change: A reviews store accepts one review per booking after checkout, hidden until both sides submit or a deadline passes. Messaging is a separate chat-style service tied to a booking, and it reuses the chat design.

steps.say: The guest sends the map area, dates, guest count and filters.
The API calls the search index. It finds listings in the area that match the filters and fit the party.
The index returns a few hundred candidate ids, ranked by relevance.
For those candidates it asks the calendar: are all the nights free? Booked ones drop out.
The API asks pricing for the total for those dates.
It loads details for the top page from the listings database and returns the results.
The guest confirms the dates and price. The app sends the quote id and an idempotency key.
The API passes the request to the booking service.
It tries to hold every night in one conditional write: set held only where the night is free. If any night is taken, the whole write fails and nothing is held.
With the hold in place, it charges the guest through the payment provider, using the idempotency key.
On success it turns the hold into a booking. On failure or timeout it releases the nights.
It publishes Confirmed on the queue, so notifications and payouts happen off the request path.
Later, the payout worker pays the host after check-in.

deepDives.title: Never double-booking a night
deepDives.question: Two guests book overlapping dates at the same moment. How do we make sure only one wins?

options.name: Check, then write
options.cons: Both checks pass before either write lands. This is a race and it will happen at scale.

options.name: Conditional write per night row
options.pros: Each night is a row. Set held only if status is free, in one atomic transaction over all nights. The store enforces it, so app bugs cannot break it.
options.cons: A long stay writes many rows. Needs a store with transactions or conditional batches.

options.name: Distributed lock on the listing
options.pros: Easy to explain: one booker at a time per listing.
options.cons: Locks expire, and a paused holder can write after losing the lock. You still need a conditional write for safety.

deepDives.because: The data itself must refuse the second booking. One row per night turns an overlap check into a simple 'is every row free' transaction. A lock can reduce contention, but never replaces the check.

deepDives.title: Availability in search
deepDives.question: How does a search for specific dates avoid showing booked listings?

options.name: Check the calendar at query time
options.pros: Always fresh and the calendar stays the single truth.
options.cons: Extra reads per search, and if most candidates are booked you have to over-fetch.

options.name: Copy availability into the index
options.pros: The index filters by date in one query. Fast.
options.cons: Every booking and host edit must update the index. It lags, and it is a large denormalised copy.

options.name: Both: coarse in the index, exact at the calendar
options.pros: The index prunes obviously busy listings. The calendar check removes the rest and fixes staleness.
options.cons: Two places to maintain. A stale index can hide a listing that is actually free.

deepDives.pick: Coarse in the index, exact check on the calendar
deepDives.because: Search can afford to be slightly stale, because the booking write is the real guard. A coarse flag such as 'any free weekend in this month' prunes most candidates, and the batched calendar check makes the shown results honest.

deepDives.title: Holding dates while paying
deepDives.question: How do we keep the nights safe during payment without locking them forever?

options.name: Book first, pay later
options.pros: Fast, and the dates are safe.
options.cons: Unpaid bookings block real guests, and cleaning up is messy.

options.name: Hold with expiry, then confirm
options.pros: Dates are held for a few minutes. If payment fails or times out, the hold lapses by itself.
options.cons: Needs expiry handling and care when payment finishes just after the hold lapses.

options.name: Pay first, book after
options.cons: You can charge a guest and then lose the dates to someone else. That means refunds.

deepDives.because: The hold is the cheap, reversible step, and payment is the costly one. Confirm only if the hold is still valid. If payment lands late, refund automatically.

deepDives.title: Paying hosts
deepDives.question: When does the host get the money, and how do we keep that safe?

options.name: Pay at booking
options.pros: Hosts like it, and it is simple.
options.cons: A cancellation or a bad stay means clawing money back.

options.name: Pay after check-in via a ledger
options.pros: The money moves only once the stay has started. Each movement is a ledger entry, so the books can be reconciled.
options.cons: Needs a ledger, scheduled payout jobs and rules for refunds.

deepDives.pick: Pay after check-in, every move in a ledger
deepDives.because: Money is where mistakes cost most. Append-only entries with idempotency keys let you replay and audit, and payouts run as queued jobs that are safe to retry.

failures.what: Two guests race for the same night
failures.impact: Without a guard, both think they booked.
failures.fix: A conditional write per night row. The loser gets a clear 'no longer available' and search refreshes the results.

failures.impact: Unknown whether the guest was charged. Nights may stay held.
failures.fix: Hold with expiry, charge with an idempotency key, and reconcile by asking the provider for the outcome of that key. Then confirm or release.

failures.impact: Results show a listing that was just booked, or hide one that just became free.
failures.fix: Treat the index as a hint. The batched calendar check and the booking write are exact. Monitor the change stream lag.

failures.what: A host edits the calendar during a booking
failures.impact: The host blocks nights that a guest is holding.
failures.fix: Host edits use the same conditional writes. Blocking a held night fails or is queued until the hold ends.

failures.impact: On retry the host could be paid twice.
failures.fix: Each payout has an id used as the provider idempotency key, and the ledger records it before the call is retried.

scaling.limit: The calendar is billions of tiny rows
scaling.lever: Shard by listing id, so one booking touches one shard. Keep only the next 1 to 2 years hot and archive past nights.
Shard the index by region. Cache popular searches for a short time, and cap how many candidates go to the calendar check.

scaling.limit: A hot listing in a busy season
scaling.lever: Conditional writes serialise per night row, which is cheap. Rate limit retries and show a quick 'taken' message.

recap.key: Search is geo plus dates, but booking is the correctness point: one calendar row per night, written conditionally so two guests cannot both win. Hold, pay with an idempotency key, then confirm.
recap.numbers: About 580 searches per second on average and 1.7K at peak, with about 35 bookings per second at peak. 2.5 billion calendar rows, around 130 GB for 7M listings a year ahead. 50 searches per booking.
moves: Geo and filter search in an index, with an exact calendar check
One calendar row per night, updated by a conditional write
Hold with expiry, charge with an idempotency key, then confirm
Quote prices once, and pay hosts after check-in through a ledger
